body_markdown:
Scabies is a contagious skin condition that has been attracting renewed attention in the UK following reports of cases in healthcare settings. The condition is caused by microscopic mites that burrow into the skin, where they can lay eggs and trigger an intensely itchy rash.


Recent reports have highlighted cases at hospitals and other community settings, raising questions about how scabies spreads, what symptoms to look for and how the infection can be treated effectively.


While scabies can be uncomfortable and persistent, it can usually be treated with appropriate medication and measures to prevent further transmission.


## What is scabies?


Scabies is a skin infection caused by tiny parasitic mites known as *Sarcoptes scabiei* . The mites burrow into the outer layers of the skin, where they can survive and reproduce.


The body's reaction to the mites, their eggs and waste can cause an allergic response. This commonly results in intense itching and a rash.


According to information cited in the supplied source, scabies can continue for weeks or even months if it is not treated correctly. Because the symptoms can resemble other skin problems, including eczema or dermatitis, some people may not immediately recognise the condition.


Scabies is not linked to poor personal hygiene. It can affect people in a variety of living environments and is primarily spread through prolonged close contact.


## Why are scabies cases attracting attention?


Reports have highlighted an increase in scabies consultations in the UK. The supplied source cites figures from the Royal College of General Practitioners' Research and Surveillance Centre indicating that scabies consultations had reached around twice the five-year national average.


Healthcare settings have also taken precautions following outbreaks. For example, the source reports that two wards at Prince Philip Hospital in Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, were closed following cases of scabies. Measures included deep cleaning and treatment for infected patients, contacts and staff.


The report also references previous cases in other healthcare and educational settings.


Although individual outbreaks can lead to additional precautions, the source notes that the risk to the wider public associated with the hospital situation was considered low.


## What are the symptoms of scabies?


Recognising the symptoms can help people seek appropriate advice and treatment.


Common symptoms include:


- Intense itching, which can be particularly troublesome at night
- A red or raised rash
- Small spots or bumps on the skin
- Irritation between the fingers
- Symptoms around the wrists, hands, feet, elbows and knees
- Rash around the waist, armpits, groin or buttocks


The rash can spread across different parts of the body. In some people, particularly older adults, young children and those with weakened immune systems, the rash may also affect the head and neck.


Symptoms may look different depending on a person's skin tone. The supplied source notes that spots can be harder to see on darker skin, although they may still be noticeable by touch.


Itching can remain severe even after treatment because the body's reaction to the mites and their waste can take time to settle.


## How does scabies spread?


Scabies is mainly transmitted through prolonged, close skin-to-skin contact. It can also spread through sharing items such as bedding, towels or clothing.


Because transmission can occur between people who live together, treating only one person may not be enough. Household members may need treatment at the same time, even if they have not developed symptoms.


Close physical contact should also be avoided while treatment is being completed.


The condition can therefore spread particularly easily in situations where people have frequent or prolonged physical contact.


## How is scabies treated?


Scabies treatment generally involves a medicated cream or lotion designed to kill the mites.


The supplied source states that treatment may be obtained through a pharmacist and should be applied according to the instructions, including to areas of the body that may sometimes be overlooked. Treatment is repeated seven days later.


Everyone in the household may need to receive treatment simultaneously. This is important because someone can potentially have scabies without obvious symptoms.


Children under two years old should not be treated with pharmacy treatments without medical advice and should be assessed by a GP.


It is also important to remember that itching can continue for several weeks after the mites have been eliminated. Persistent itching does not automatically mean that treatment has failed.


## How can you prevent scabies from spreading?


Alongside medication, environmental measures can help reduce the risk of passing scabies to other people.


The source recommends washing bedding and clothing at 60°C or above on the first day of treatment. Where possible, items can also be placed in a hot dryer.


Clothing and other items that cannot be washed can be sealed in a bag for at least three days. This allows time for mites to die.


People with scabies should avoid sharing towels, clothes or bedding with others. Close physical contact, including sexual contact, should also be avoided until the recommended course of treatment has been completed.


These steps are particularly important when several people in the same household are affected.


## When should you speak to a doctor?


Medical advice is recommended in several situations.


You should contact a GP if a child under two has symptoms of scabies, particularly if someone else in the household has the condition.


Medical advice may also be appropriate if you believe the skin has become infected, if you have another skin condition such as eczema, or if you develop a crusted or flaky rash affecting areas such as the hands, feet, knees or elbows.


The supplied source also advises seeking medical attention if itching continues between two and four weeks after completing pharmacy treatment.


## Can scabies last after treatment?


Yes. One of the most important things to understand about scabies is that itching may continue even after successful treatment.


The mites can be killed relatively quickly with appropriate treatment, but the skin's inflammatory response can take longer to disappear.


However, continuing or worsening symptoms should not simply be ignored. If symptoms persist beyond the expected recovery period, medical advice can help determine whether further treatment is necessary or whether another skin condition could be responsible.


## Final thoughts


Scabies can cause significant discomfort, but recognising the symptoms and following treatment instructions can help control the infection and reduce its spread.


The most common warning signs include intense nighttime itching and a raised or spotty rash, particularly around the hands, fingers, wrists and other affected areas. Because scabies can resemble other skin conditions, professional advice can be useful when the diagnosis is uncertain.


If someone in a household develops scabies, treating household members at the same time and washing or isolating potentially affected clothing and bedding are important parts of preventing further transmission.

Information about symptoms and treatment can vary between individuals. If you think you may have scabies, are concerned about your symptoms, or are treating a young child, speak with a pharmacist, GP or other qualified healthcare professional.
